newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rejects rebel demands, steps up pressure.
newsitem.headline: Peru rejects rebel demands, steps up pressure.

text.p: Peru stepped up pressure on Marxist gunmen holding 73 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home and refused to start talks to end the 37-day crisis unless the rebels dropped demands for the release of jailed comrades.
Police intensified their war of nerves on Wednesday with the 15-odd Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holed up inside the residence.

Undeterred by a burst of warning shots from the residence in the early hours, police circled a helicopter above the diplomatic compound and moved in black armoured personnel carriers with heavy machineguns to within two blocks.
President Alberto Fujimori said the government would not sit down to talks with the MRTA unless it withdrew its main demand.

"We are not going to allow (government negotiator Domingo) Palermo to go to the negotiating table unless they accept that there will be no release of prisoners," Fujimori said at a meeting with Japanese reporters, a recording of which was later released.
Palermo has not met with rebels since a first face-to-face encounter on Dec. 28.

Fujimori, whose younger brother Pedro is among the captives, said the government could consider other MRTA demands for improved jail conditions and political asylum in another country. "It is a question of listening and giving suggestions," he said.

The white police helicopter made three series of flyovers, including one night-flight with its lights switched off. It swept low between buildings around the residence, before gaining height each of the roughly 15 times it flew directly over the compound.
The helicopter did not buzz the building, but the rebels would have seen a policemen perched at its open door holding a machinegun.
After the first flyover, two Russian-made Caspir armoured personnel carriers drove around the residence and parked nearby, one aiming its machinegun toward the compound.

The helicopter and vehicle movements followed a day of unusual police maneuvres on Tuesday during which several policemen ran up and down past the compound's front gate and at least one threw stones onto the driveway in an apparent attempt to provoke a reaction from the rebels.

The rebels, who are armed with AKM assault rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the compound against surprise attack, responded by firing at least five rounds into the night air early on Wednesday.
Following the heightened police activity at the site Wednesday, the International Committee of the Red Cross said it would reduce its visits to the residence for safety reasons.

"The security situation has obliged the Red Cross to limit for the moment its presence within the residence," Red Cross spokeswoman Cecilia Baux told Reuters. "However, we will continue covering the hostages' basic needs."

The Red Cross will now limit itself to delivering meals and cleaning materials. The restrictions, however, were not expected to affect the Red Cross' role as a go-between for the rebels and the government.
President Alberto Fujimori claimed the moves were necessary for the police to control the siege site properly.
"The responsibility of the police is to have control of the street. There is no provocation. If it happens to irritate, that is not part of the strategy," he said.
Fujimori has not ruled out using force against the rebels, if they harm any of the hostages.

But Fujimori's tough talk and increased police activity seemed to make little impression on the jungle-trained gunmen who put out a new banner on the roof of the residence early Wednesday that read: "Surrender is not the path for Tupac Amaru followers."

The rebels, who take the name for their movement from an 18th century Indian leader who led an uprising against Spanish colonial rule, originally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a garden cocktail party at the residence Dec. 17.

They released most in what they called "goodwill gestures" keeping those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including two Peruvian ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors.
